item.research_question: How does the processing temperature (77 K vs. 300 K) during high-pressure torsion (HPT) affect the microstructure evolution, phase stability, and mechanical properties (hardness and tensile strength) of the Co20Cr26Fe20Mn20Ni14 high-entropy alloy, particularly regarding the phenomenon of natural aging?
item.material_system: Co20Cr26Fe20Mn20Ni14 high-entropy alloy (low stacking fault energy of 3.5 mJ/m2)
item.processing_route: High-pressure torsion (HPT) at 77 K (cryogenic) and 300 K (room temperature) under 5 GPa pressure for 1, 3, and 5 anvil turns; samples held for natural aging up to two months.
item.test_conditions: Vickers hardness (300 g load, 10 s dwell) measured at 10 min, 1 day, 2 weeks, 1 month, and 2 months post-processing; tensile testing (strain rate 10^-3 s^-1) conducted 2 weeks post-processing; XRD, SEM, EBSD, and TEM analysis performed.
key_findings: Cryogenic HPT resulted in lower mechanical strength (hardness and tensile strength) compared to room temperature HPT after natural aging.
Vickers hardness of cryo-HPT samples dropped precipitously after two weeks of natural aging, whereas room temperature HPT samples showed no hardness decrease over one month.
Deformation-induced FCC-to-HCP phase transformation occurred in the alloy processed by cryo-HPT, confirmed by XRD and TEM.
Dislocation density in cryo-HPT samples was very high (~1.0 to 2.5 × 10^16 m^-2) immediately after processing but decreased significantly with natural aging time.
Room temperature HPT produced an average grain size of 61 ± 25 nm, while cryo-HPT resulted in larger average grain sizes (e.g., 5.42 ± 1.69 μm after 5 turns).
The volume fraction of deformation twins decreased from 48% in the annealed state to 0.6% after 5 turns of cryo-HPT.
The σ phase peaks observed in the annealed state almost disappeared after HPT processing at both 77 K and 300 K.
item.mechanism: The authors attribute the lower strength and hardness drop in cryo-HPT samples to 'self-annealing' (static recovery and static recrystallization) during natural aging, driven by the high stored energy from deformation and the low stacking fault energy which inhibits cross-slip and dynamic recrystallization during processing but allows static recovery afterward. The FCC-to-HCP transformation is rationalized as a kinetically possible transition due to high pressure and low temperature overcoming the energy barrier.
item.limitations: The authors note that extreme grain refinement during cryo-HPT cannot be entirely ruled out, as nano-grained structures might have been unstable at room temperature and underwent recovery before characterization.
quotes: Cryogenic HPT was found to result in a lower mechanical strength of alloy Co20Cr26Fe20Mn20Ni14 than room temperature HPT.
The observed decrease of the dislocation density with natural aging time for all numbers of anvil revolutions of cryo-HPT is seen as a clear indication of self-annealing.
The occurrence of an HPT-induced FCC to HCP phase transformation may be rationalized using an analogy with the mechanism proposed by Talonen and Hänninen for low SFE stainless steel.
